title: Writing custom middleware (InvokeAsync pattern)
hook: Custom middleware is a class or lambda with InvokeAsync that receives HttpContext and the next RequestDelegate — the standard extension point for cross-cutting concerns like correlation IDs, tenant resolution, or request logging.

blocks.text: Custom middleware implements cross-cutting logic that runs for many requests. The conventional pattern is a class with constructor injecting RequestDelegate _next and optional singleton services, plus InvokeAsync(HttpContext context) or InvokeAsync(HttpContext, IMyService) for per-request dependencies. Register with app.UseMiddleware<T>() or inline app.Use(async (context, next) => ...).

entries.plainDefinition: Entry point the pipeline calls. Must call await _next(context) to continue unless short-circuiting.
entries.example: public async Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext context) { await _next(context); }

entries.plainDefinition: Factory-activated middleware resolved per request via IMiddlewareFactory — preferred for scoped constructor injection.
Registers convention-based middleware class with DI activating constructor parameters.
The next link in the chain passed to middleware constructor or Use lambda.

blocks.text: Filters and endpoint code belong to specific routes; middleware runs earlier for all matching pipeline branches. Correlation IDs must be set before logging and outbound HTTP calls. Tenant resolution from subdomain belongs in middleware so DbContext and services see the same tenant for the whole request. Interviewers ask you to implement logging middleware or explain IMiddleware vs convention-based class.

blocks.title: When to use middleware vs filter
blocks.body: Middleware: transport concerns, headers, timing, early auth enrichment. Filters: MVC model binding, validation, action-specific behavior. Minimal APIs have no action filters — middleware or endpoint filters (.NET 7+) apply.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Host builds pipeline at startup
items.body: UseMiddleware<T> registers T with a factory that captures _next.

items.title: Per request: resolve middleware instance
items.body: Convention-based: one instance per app (singleton). IMiddleware: created per request.

items.title: DI injects InvokeAsync parameters
items.body: Method parameters resolved per request from RequestServices — correct place for scoped services.

diagram.title: Custom middleware in the pipeline
diagram.source:
flowchart LR
  REQ[Request] --> CM[Custom Middleware\nInvokeAsync pre]
  CM --> NEXT[await _next]
  NEXT --> INNER[Routing / Auth / Endpoint]
  INNER --> POST[InvokeAsync post]
  POST --> RES[Response]

snippet.label: Correlation ID middleware — production pattern
snippet.explanation: Reads or generates correlation ID, adds response header on starting, scopes all logs in the request. Register early after exception handler.

snippet.label: IMiddleware for per-request activation
snippet.explanation: IMiddleware is instantiated per request via IMiddlewareFactory — safe for scoped dependencies in the middleware class itself if needed.

snippet.label: Extension method for clean Program.cs
snippet.explanation: Extension methods mirror framework UseAuthentication style — packages ship middleware as one line for consumers.

snippet.label: Unit test middleware in isolation
snippet.explanation: Test pre/post behavior without Kestrel by mocking DefaultHttpContext and a flag next delegate — faster than full integration tests for header logic.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Forgetting await next(context) so the pipeline stops. Injecting scoped services in middleware constructor on convention-based class — captive dependency bug. Writing to response body before await next then calling next — double response. Not using OnStarting for headers when endpoint may set status late.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: structured logs should include CorrelationId from middleware scope on every line — grep one ID across API and downstream calls. OpenTelemetry ActivitySource in middleware sets baggage propagated to HttpClient. If p95 latency grows, timing middleware before and after await next isolates endpoint vs post-processing. Memory leaks from middleware holding HttpContext beyond request — never store context in static fields.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Hot path — factory overhead negligible but measurable

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Cannot write basic InvokeAsync with await _next. Injecting DbContext in middleware constructor without explaining captive dependency. Not knowing IMiddleware exists. Saying middleware and filters are interchangeable for minimal APIs.

interviewTakeaways: Custom middleware: constructor takes RequestDelegate _next; InvokeAsync calls await _next(context) unless short-circuiting.
Inject scoped services via InvokeAsync parameters or IMiddleware — never scoped in singleton constructor.
Production tip: correlation ID middleware early; scope logs; OnStarting for response headers.
60s: InvokeAsync pattern with _next. IMiddleware for per-request activation. Method injection for scoped deps. Express app.use is the same onion. Extension method for registration ergonomics.
Follow-up: difference between convention-based middleware and IMiddleware activation?
commonPitfalls: Scoped DbContext in middleware constructor gets you rejected — captive dependency, wrong tenant data.
Missing await next() silently hangs or returns empty responses.
Strong answer: 'RequestDelegate in ctor. Scoped deps on InvokeAsync or IMiddleware. Correlation ID via OnStarting. Unit test with DefaultHttpContext.'
introducedIn: ASP.NET Core 1.0; IMiddleware in ASP.NET Core 2.0

jsTsCorrelations.note: Express middleware is a function closing over nothing — state comes from req. ASP.NET middleware is a class with _next captured at pipeline build; per-request state lives on HttpContext.
Fastify hooks run in declared order like middleware layers. ASP.NET InvokeAsync pre/post around await _next matches onRequest + onResponse hook pair.
